steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: One bag has three packs. Each pack has three boxes. Each box has three sweets. Three keeps multiplying itself as you count through the layers.

steps.title: Combine powers with the same base
steps.narration: Keep the base and add the powers when you multiply. When you divide powers with the same nonzero base, subtract the bottom exponent from the top.

steps.title: Apply an outer power
steps.narration: Multiply the exponents when you raise a power to another power. An outer power also applies to each factor of a product and each part of a quotient.

steps.title: Use zero and negative powers
steps.narration: Any nonzero base to the power zero gives one. A negative exponent takes the reciprocal. You can see why when you divide equal powers and get one.

steps.title: Read a fractional exponent as a root
steps.narration: For a positive base, the denominator gives the root and the numerator gives the power. Take the root first if that makes the numbers easier to handle.

steps.title: Match the bases before solving
steps.narration: If you can rewrite both sides as powers of the same positive base other than one, equate their exponents. This turns many index equations into simple algebra.

steps.title: Normalise standard form
steps.narration: Give a nonzero number an integer power of ten and a coefficient with magnitude from one up to ten. For products or quotients, handle the coefficients and powers separately. For sums or differences, match the powers first. Then normalise.

steps.title: Spot the fraction in the power
steps.narration: The denominator of the exponent is four, so start by finding the fourth root of sixteen.

steps.title: Use the numerator as a power
steps.narration: The numerator is three, so cube the root you just found. Two cubed gives eight.

steps.title: Take the reciprocal
steps.narration: The exponent was negative, so take the reciprocal of eight to get one eighth.

steps.title: Rewrite using base three
steps.narration: The right side already uses base three. Twenty-seven is three cubed and nine is three squared, so use base three on the left as well.

steps.title: Multiply the inner and outer powers
steps.narration: Both powers on the left have an outer exponent. Multiply the inner exponent by the entire expression in its bracket.

steps.title: Subtract the whole denominator exponent
steps.narration: Division subtracts the denominator exponent. Keep the brackets until you have subtracted both terms in that exponent.

steps.title: Compare the exponents
steps.narration: With base three on both sides, the exponents must agree. Subtract x from both sides, then check that both exponents become eight.

steps.title: Check both exponents
steps.narration: A value that looks close must still make both exponents equal. Three gives seven on one side and six on the other.

steps.title: Check the sign in standard form
steps.narration: After multiplying the two decimals, check the size of your answer. Eight point six must be divided by ten to give zero point eight six.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.narration: Keep track of what happens to the base and its exponent before you do the arithmetic.

quickCheck.stem: Write \frac{0.0001432}{1940000} as k × 10^{n}, where 1 ≤ k < 10 and n is an integer. Give k to three decimal places.

options.why: The coefficient rounds to 7.381 after normalising the quotient, and the power of ten is −11.
Dividing the powers gives 10^{-10} before normalising, so a positive exponent has the wrong scale.
A power of 2 would make the quotient much larger than 1, although the numerator is smaller than the denominator.
The exponent is right, but 1.432 ÷ 1.94 ≈ 0.738144, which normalises to a coefficient of 7.381.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: You start with one sweet and double your pile each round. When you reach eight sweets, a logarithm tells you how many doublings it took.

steps.title: Read a logarithm as an exponent
working: log A = log_{10} A in common logarithm notation; ln A = log_{e} A
steps.narration: A logarithm asks what power of the base gives the argument. The base must be positive and different from one, and the argument must be positive.

steps.title: Combine logs with the same base
steps.narration: Add logs of the same base by multiplying the positive arguments. Subtract logs of the same base by dividing the first argument by the second.

steps.title: Move a multiplier into the power
steps.narration: A number multiplying a logarithm can move inside as an exponent on the positive argument. This works for fractional and negative multipliers as well.

steps.title: Change to a convenient base
steps.narration: Choose a valid new base and use it in both logarithms. Put the original argument on top and the original base underneath.

steps.title: Solve within the original domain
steps.display: log_{b} u = log_{b} v ⇒ u = v (u > 0, v > 0)
steps.narration: Combine same-base logs, then equate positive arguments or rewrite a single log as an exponential equation. Test each candidate in the original equation, where every argument must be positive.

steps.title: Start with the allowed values
steps.narration: Both arguments must be positive. The stricter condition is that x must be greater than two.

steps.title: Combine and undo the logarithm
steps.narration: Addition combines the arguments into a product. Now use the meaning of a log to lift two to the third power.

steps.title: Factor and test the candidates
steps.narration: The quadratic gives four and minus two. Only four is greater than two, and it makes the original logs add up to three.

steps.title: Start with the first log
steps.narration: The bases differ, so find each exponent on its own. Three to the third power gives twenty-seven.

steps.title: Find the power of a fractional base
steps.narration: The base is one quarter. A negative exponent flips it to four, and the third power gives sixty-four.

steps.title: Find the denominator
steps.narration: Eighty-one is three to the fourth power. Its reciprocal takes a negative exponent, so the denominator is minus four.

steps.title: Keep both negative signs
steps.narration: Subtracting minus three makes the numerator six. The denominator is negative, so the simplified quotient is minus three halves.

steps.title: Halve the argument using division inside the log
steps.narration: Halving the logarithm would take the square root of ten inside it. To halve ten itself, subtract the logarithm of two instead.

steps.title: Check the sign of a reciprocal power
steps.narration: Check which power actually makes the argument. Three to the fourth gives eighty-one, and the negative fourth power gives its reciprocal.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.narration: Read every logarithm as a question about a power, and keep its base and argument in view.

options.why: The three powers are 3, 4 and 2 exactly. Their signed sum is 5, so there is no rounding to 6.
The two positive terms add to 7. Subtracting 2 gives 5.
Four is the middle logarithm alone. The other terms contribute 3 − 2 = 1.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: Imagine bundles of sticks tied in pairs. Pull out the complete pairs first, then see which loose bundles have the same label and can go together.

steps.title: Take perfect squares out of roots
steps.narration: Find a perfect-square factor under the root and bring its nonnegative square root outside. A square root that stays irrational, like root two, is a surd.

steps.title: Add and subtract like surds
steps.narration: Simplify each root first. When the numbers under the roots agree, add or subtract the coefficients and keep the shared root.

steps.title: Multiply and divide under the root
steps.narration: Multiply the outside numbers together and the numbers under the roots together. For division, you can combine nonnegative roots under one root when the bottom root is positive.

steps.title: Clear a single root from the denominator
steps.narration: Multiply the top and bottom by the same root. That keeps the fraction equal and leaves an ordinary number underneath.

steps.title: Clear a two-term denominator with its conjugate
steps.narration: For two terms in a denominator, reverse the sign between them and multiply the top and bottom by that conjugate. The middle terms cancel.

steps.title: Look for square factors
steps.narration: Both roots on top contain a perfect square times five. Split them up so that the shared root is visible.

steps.title: Subtract the coefficients
steps.narration: The roots now match, so subtract two from three and keep the root of five.

steps.title: Cancel the remaining root
steps.narration: The top and bottom are the same nonzero number. That means the whole fraction equals one.

steps.title: Choose a conjugate
steps.narration: The bottom has two roots joined by addition. Choose root three minus root two so the squared terms will leave a positive one.

steps.title: Multiply both parts of the fraction
steps.narration: Use the same factor on top and bottom to keep the fraction equal. Now distribute each term on top across the second bracket.

steps.title: Collect the like terms
steps.narration: Two root six plus root six gives three root six. The ordinary numbers add to minus seven, and division by one leaves the result.

steps.title: Simplify before subtracting
steps.narration: A difference of two roots cannot be taken by subtracting inside the root. Expose the common root of three and subtract the outside numbers.

steps.title: Keep the signs when expanding
steps.narration: Check the plain numbers separately from the roots. Both plain products are negative here, so they give minus seven.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.narration: Pull out square factors first so you can see which roots combine and how to clear the denominator.

options.why: The conjugate gives 3^{2} − 5 = 4 in the denominator, so 2 is too small.
Multiplying by 3 + \sqrt{5} above and below gives (1 − \sqrt{5}) divided by 4.
The original numerator is negative and its denominator is positive, so a positive result cannot match.
The root terms in the numerator are 2\sqrt{5} − 3\sqrt{5}, giving −\sqrt{5}.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: You have six oranges and nine mangoes. Make three identical bags with two oranges and three mangoes each. Factoring spots what every bag has in common.

steps.title: Take out a common factor by grouping
steps.narration: Take out what every term shares. If no factor appears in every term, try grouping terms until the groups share a whole bracket.

steps.title: Recognise special factors
steps.narration: When one square is subtracted from another, put their square roots in brackets with opposite signs. A perfect-square trinomial gives a repeated bracket. For cubes, keep the sign in the first factor and flip it in the middle term of the second.

steps.title: Split the middle term and solve
steps.display: ax^{2} + bx + c = ax^{2} + mx + nx + c
steps.narration: Choose two numbers that multiply to the leading coefficient times the constant and add to the middle coefficient. Group the four terms, then set each factor to zero if the product equals zero.

steps.title: Use the quadratic formula and discriminant
steps.narration: For a quadratic set equal to zero, use its signed coefficients. The expression under the root is the discriminant. Positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives a repeated root, and negative gives no real roots.

sources.where: The quadratic formula and the discriminant

steps.title: Link the roots to the coefficients
working: ax^{2} + bx + c = a(x − α)(x − β)
steps.narration: If the two roots are alpha and beta, their sum is minus the middle coefficient over the leading coefficient. Their product is the constant over the leading coefficient.

steps.title: Get the remainder by substitution
working: x + 1 is a factor of P(x)
steps.narration: When you divide by x minus a number, substitute that number to get the remainder. A zero remainder means the divisor is a factor, so the other roots come from the quotient.

steps.title: Put zero on one side
steps.narration: Bring all the terms to one side so the other side is zero. That lets you use the zero product rule after factorising.

steps.title: Find two numbers to split the middle
steps.narration: The leading coefficient times the constant gives minus twelve. The middle coefficient is minus one, so split it into three and minus four.

steps.title: Group and read off the roots
steps.narration: Both groups contain the same bracket. Take it out, then set each of the two factors equal to zero to find the roots.

steps.title: Turn the known root into a factor
steps.display: One root of x^{3} − 2x^{2} − 5x + 6 = 0 is 1. Find the other roots.
steps.narration: A root of one makes the polynomial zero, so x minus one is a factor. Taking it out will leave a quadratic.

steps.title: Remove the known factor by grouping
steps.narration: Split the middle terms so you can group the cubic into pieces that all contain x minus one. Take that common factor out.

steps.title: Factor the remaining quadratic
steps.narration: Minus three and two multiply to minus six and add to minus one, so they give the constants in these brackets.

steps.title: Set the remaining factors to zero
steps.narration: Set each remaining bracket equal to zero. Either factor can make the product zero, giving three and minus two as the other roots.

steps.title: Keep the entire second square in brackets
steps.narration: A minus before a bracket changes both signs inside it. The first bracket therefore has minus a and plus b.

steps.title: Substitute the root, with its correct sign
steps.narration: Set the factor equal to zero before substituting. Four makes x minus four zero, so use four in the polynomial.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.display: Use the product to find the roots
steps.narration: Factor into simpler pieces, then set each factor equal to zero when the product is zero.

quickCheck.stem: For which p does x^{2} − (p−2)x + 2p + 1 = 0 have equal roots?

options.why: The discriminant is (p − 2)^{2} − 4(2p + 1) = p(p − 12), so it vanishes at 0 and 12.
Neither 1 nor 2 makes p(p − 12) equal to zero.
Zero works, but 21 leaves a nonzero discriminant and gives two distinct roots.
Both 4 and 5 make p(p − 12) negative, so neither gives equal real roots.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: Two bags each hold an orange and a mango. Open both bags and put oranges with oranges and mangoes with mangoes. Algebra sorts terms that way too.

steps.title: Expand, then collect matching terms
steps.narration: Multiply each term by every term in the other bracket, keeping its sign. Collect terms only when their letters and powers match.

steps.title: Cancel common factors and keep restrictions
steps.narration: First exclude every value that makes an original denominator zero. Factor the top and bottom, then cancel a shared nonzero factor from the whole numerator and denominator.

steps.title: Use the appropriate fraction operation
working: Original denominators and any divisor must be nonzero.
steps.narration: Use a common denominator to add or subtract. For multiplication, multiply top by top and bottom by bottom. For division, multiply by the reciprocal of the nonzero divisor.

steps.title: Undo operations to change the subject
working: y = ax + bx + c ⇒ x = \frac{y − c}{a + b} (a + b ≠ 0)
steps.narration: Use the same inverse operation on both sides. If the new subject appears more than once, collect its terms on one side, factor it out, then divide by its nonzero coefficient.

steps.title: Solve two equations together
steps.narration: For elimination, match the coefficients of one variable and add or subtract to remove it. For substitution, isolate one variable and replace it in the other equation. Check the pair in both equations.

steps.title: Substitute in a linear and quadratic system
steps.narration: Use the linear equation to replace one variable in the quadratic. Solve the resulting equation, then find the matching second coordinate for every root and check both equations.

steps.title: Look for a variable to eliminate
steps.narration: The y terms have equal size and opposite signs. Add the two equations so those terms cancel.

steps.title: Find the first unknown
steps.narration: Only x remains after adding. Divide both sides by three to find the value of x.

steps.title: Substitute and check the pair
steps.narration: Put three into the simpler equation to find y. Check the pair in the first equation as well, since it must satisfy both.

steps.title: Keep the original restrictions
steps.narration: Keep the four excluded values in view throughout. They make an original denominator zero, even if some factors later disappear.

steps.title: Factor each expression
steps.narration: Both denominators are differences of squares. The second numerator has a common factor of x, so factor it as well.

steps.title: Cancel matching factors
steps.narration: Cancel x minus three and x minus seven, because each is a whole factor above and below. The original restrictions still apply.

steps.title: Cancel the same bracket
steps.narration: The numerator contains x minus three, so cancel the matching minus bracket underneath. The plus bracket is a different factor.

steps.title: Collect terms with their signs
steps.narration: Moving the negative term from the left adds it on the right. Both terms on the right containing the subject then contribute a plus sign.

steps.title: Answer what the question asks for
steps.narration: If a question asks for x plus y, finding x is only part of the work. Substitute both values into the requested expression.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.narration: Keep each expression equivalent and use the same operation on both sides of an equation.

quickCheck.stem: Make g the subject of gt^{2} − k − w = 0, with t ≠ 0.

options.why: Both k and w are added to the other side, and the coefficient of g is t^{2}.
Adding k and w and dividing by the nonzero coefficient t^{2} isolates g.
The denominator is right, but moving −w requires adding w to both sides.
The coefficient multiplying g is t^{2}, so dividing by t alone leaves another factor of t.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: How steep is the hill here?
steps.narration: Imagine cycling up a hill that gets steeper and then flattens out. Differentiation tells you how steep the road is just where your front wheel sits.

steps.title: Find the slope from first principles
steps.narration: The derivative is the gradient of the tangent and the instantaneous rate of change. To find it from first principles, take the limit of the gradient between two nearby points as their separation approaches zero.

steps.title: Differentiate powers term by term
working: y′(x_{0}) is the tangent gradient at x_{0}
steps.narration: Bring the exponent down as a multiplier and reduce it by one wherever the power is differentiable. Keep constant multipliers, differentiate sums and differences term by term, and replace any standalone constant by zero.

steps.title: Use the product rule
steps.narration: When two functions are multiplied, differentiate the first while keeping the second, then keep the first and differentiate the second. Add the two results.

steps.title: Use the quotient rule
steps.narration: Keep the order in the numerator. Multiply the derivative of the top by the bottom, subtract the top times the derivative of the bottom, and square the bottom.

steps.title: Use the chain rule for a function inside a function
working: (sin x)′ = cos x; (cos x)′ = −sin x; (tan x)′ = sec^{2} x
steps.narration: Differentiate the outside while leaving the inside in place, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. In radians, sine gives cosine, cosine gives minus sine, and tangent gives secant squared.

steps.title: Find and classify stationary points
steps.display: f′(c) = 0; f′′(c) < 0 gives a local maximum
working: f′ changes from + to − for a maximum, and from − to + for a minimum
Interior critical points have a zero or undefined derivative
steps.narration: A negative second derivative at a stationary point gives a local maximum and a positive one gives a local minimum. If it is zero, check for a change in slope sign. On a closed interval, compare endpoints and interior critical points.

steps.title: Find the gradient function
steps.display: Find the gradient of y = 2x^{3} − 5x + 1 at x = 2.
steps.narration: The question asks for the slope at a particular point. Find the derivative first so it can give the slope for any x.

steps.title: Use the specified point
steps.narration: Put two into the derivative. The square is worked out before multiplying by six.

steps.title: Read the slope
steps.narration: The gradient is positive nineteen, so the tangent slopes upwards as you move to the right.

steps.title: Expand the quadratic
steps.display: At what x does f(x) = x(4 − x) reach its maximum?
steps.narration: This product expands into a simple quadratic. Expanding makes it easy to differentiate each term separately.

steps.title: Find the horizontal tangent
steps.narration: At the top of this smooth curve the gradient is zero. Set four minus two x equal to zero to find where that happens.

steps.title: Check that it is the maximum
steps.narration: The second derivative is negative throughout, so the slope decreases through zero and the parabola reaches its maximum at two.

steps.title: Keep the inner derivative
steps.narration: After differentiating the outer cube, keep going. The inside has derivative two, so the whole result must be multiplied by two.

steps.title: Track both minus signs
steps.narration: The minus in front of the reciprocal stays in place, and the negative exponent supplies another minus. Together they make the reciprocal term positive in the derivative.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.narration: Differentiate for the gradient, then use the point or the slope condition the question gives you.

options.why: Multiplying by the old powers gives 12x^{2} and −4x, and differentiating x gives 1.
The cubic needs a multiplier of 3, and the quadratic needs a multiplier of 2.
The cubic contributes 4 × 3, so the first coefficient is 12.
The term −2x^{2} contributes −2 × 2 × x, so its derivative is −4x.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Build the whole from thin strips
steps.narration: Imagine covering a curved patch of ground with strips of paper. Thinner strips fit the edge better. An integral gives the exact total as the strips get thinner.

steps.title: Reverse differentiation
steps.display: F′(x) = f(x) ⇒ ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C on an interval
steps.narration: Integration finds a function whose derivative gives the original expression. Add a constant for an indefinite integral, because differentiating any constant gives zero. Use a given point to find it.

steps.title: Add one to the power, then divide
steps.narration: Raise the exponent by one, then divide by that new exponent. Integrate each term separately and keep any constant multiplier. The reciprocal power uses a logarithm.

steps.title: Check simple substitutions by differentiating
working: ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C; ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C; ∫ sec^{2} x dx = tan x + C
steps.narration: When the inside is linear, divide by its slope after integrating the outside. Differentiate your result as a check. The chain rule should multiply that slope back in.

steps.title: Use upper value minus lower value
steps.narration: For a continuous function, use an antiderivative and subtract its value at the lower limit from its value at the upper limit. The constant cancels.

steps.title: Use nonnegative heights for area
working: A = ∫_{a}^{b} (upper − lower) dx when their order stays fixed
A between y = x and the axis on [−1, 1] is \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1
steps.narration: Below the horizontal axis a definite integral counts negatively, so split at any sign change and add the positive areas. Between two curves, split where they cross and integrate upper minus lower on each interval.

steps.title: Find an antiderivative
steps.display: A curve has gradient 4x − 3 and passes through (1, 2). Find its equation.
steps.narration: The gradient is the derivative of the curve, so integrate it to recover the equation up to a constant.

steps.title: Use the point to find the constant
steps.narration: The point tells you which curve you need. At x equal to one, y is two, so use those values to solve for the constant.

steps.title: Write and check the curve
steps.narration: Differentiate the equation to get the given gradient, and put one in place of x to check the point.

steps.title: Find where the curves meet
steps.display: Find the area bounded by y = 4 − x^{2} and y = 2x + 1.
steps.narration: The region starts and ends where the curves meet. Equate their y values and factor the resulting quadratic to get the limits.

steps.title: Find the upper curve
steps.narration: Zero lies between the crossings. At zero, the parabola is higher, and the order stays the same between those two crossings.

steps.title: Integrate the height
steps.narration: Add up the heights over the interval by integrating. Treat each term separately and keep its sign.

steps.title: Subtract the lower value
steps.narration: Substitute both limits with care. Subtracting the negative lower value adds nine, giving ten and two thirds square units.

steps.title: Keep the sign of a definite integral
steps.narration: The expression is negative throughout this interval. The definite integral keeps that sign, so upper value minus lower value gives minus eleven thirds.

steps.title: Divide by the inner slope
steps.narration: The usual power step gives a factor of two thirds. The inside has slope two, so divide by two as well.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.display: Reverse the derivative and use the given information
steps.narration: Find an antiderivative, then use the limits for a definite integral or a given point to fix the constant.

quickCheck.stem: A curve has gradient 6x − 5 at every point and passes through (2, 5). Find its equation.

options.why: Its derivative is 12x − 5, so the coefficient of x squared is too large.
Its derivative is 12x + 5, so both derivative terms differ from the given gradient.
The derivative is right, but substituting x = 2 gives −3 instead of 5.
Its derivative is 6x − 5 and substituting x = 2 gives 12 − 10 + 3 = 5.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Walk it, cover it, fill it
steps.narration: Walk round a garden to measure its edge, lay mats to cover the ground, or fill a bucket with water. Each job measures something different.

steps.title: Add lengths for the distance round
steps.narration: Perimeter measures the full boundary in length units. Add each outside edge once. For a circle, multiply twice the radius by pi.

steps.title: Measure flat area with the correct height
steps.narration: Area measures a flat region in square units. Use perpendicular height with the base. For a trapezium, use the average of the parallel side lengths times their perpendicular distance.

steps.title: Take the right fraction of a circle
steps.narration: Divide the central angle in degrees by three hundred and sixty to get the fraction of a full turn. Apply that fraction to the circumference for arc length and to the circle area for sector area.

sources.where: Calculation Notes, Sectors and Areas of segments

steps.title: Find the area and boundary of a segment
steps.narration: The smaller segment is what remains after taking the triangle out of the sector. Its boundary is the arc and chord. Bisect the central angle to find half the chord, then double it.
working: L_{chord} = 2r sin(\frac{θ}{2}); P_{minor segment} = L_{arc} + L_{chord}

sources.where: Calculation Notes, Sectors and Areas of segments

steps.title: Use the base area for volume
working: B = 6 cm^{2}, h = 8 cm ⇒ V_{prism} = 48 cm^{3}
steps.narration: Multiply the base area by the perpendicular height for a prism or cylinder. A pyramid or cone takes a third of that product. A hemisphere takes half the volume of the matching sphere.

sources.where: Surface area of a right pyramid, Surface area of a cone, and The sphere

steps.title: Add the exposed surfaces
working: S_{cuboid} = 2(lw + lh + wh); S_{prism} = 2B + P_{base}h for a right prism
ℓ = \sqrt{r^{2} + h^{2}} for a right cone
steps.narration: For total surface area, add the curved surfaces and any exposed flat faces. The cone uses slant height for its curved area. For a solid hemisphere, include the flat circular base.

sources.where: Surface area of a right pyramid, Surface area of a cone, and The sphere

steps.title: Use the triangle at the end
steps.display: A right triangular prism is 5 cm long. Its right-angled end has perpendicular sides 3 cm and 4 cm. Find its volume.
steps.narration: Look at the triangular end first. Its perpendicular sides give a base and height for the triangle area.

steps.title: Extend that area through the prism
steps.narration: A prism has the same end area all the way along its length, so multiply that area by five.

steps.title: Give the volume in cubic units
steps.narration: The area has square centimetres and the length has centimetres. Their product gives thirty cubic centimetres for the volume.

steps.title: Find the fraction of a full turn
steps.display: A 45° sector of a circle has radius 8 cm. What is its perimeter?
steps.narration: Forty-five degrees is one eighth of a full turn, so the arc is one eighth of the full circumference.

steps.title: Find the curved edge
steps.narration: The circumference is sixteen pi centimetres. Take one eighth of it because that is the part around the curved edge.

steps.title: Include the straight edges
steps.narration: Walk the entire boundary of the sector in your mind. It has the curved edge and two straight radii, each eight centimetres long.

steps.title: Count the whole sector boundary
steps.display: Wrong  P = 2π cm     |     Right  P = (16 + 2π) cm
steps.narration: The arc measures only the curved part. Add both straight radii whenever the question asks for the perimeter of the sector.

steps.title: Use the area of the actual prism end
steps.display: Right triangular end with perpendicular sides 3 cm and 4 cm
steps.narration: A triangular end takes half the product of its perpendicular sides. Use that area times the prism length to avoid treating the end as a rectangle.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.display: Match the formula to what is measured
steps.narration: Trace the boundary for perimeter, cover the surface for area, and fill the space for volume.

quickCheck.stem: Find the area of a sector with centre angle 70° and radius 6 cm. Use π ≈ \frac{22}{7}.

options.why: The specified fraction of the circle area is (70 ÷ 360) × (22 ÷ 7) × 36, which is 22 cm^{2}.
This is twice the sector area. The sector takes only 70 out of the full 360 degrees.
This is three times the sector area. The angle fraction must be 70 divided by 360.
This is four times the sector area. Multiplying the circle area by 70 divided by 360 gives 22.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Two ways to grow a pile
steps.narration: Start with a pile of sweets. In one game you add two each round. In another you double the pile. Both patterns are predictable.

steps.title: Recognise an arithmetic progression by its difference
steps.narration: An arithmetic progression adds the same difference each time. The first term is a, so there are one fewer jumps than the position of the term.

steps.title: Sum an arithmetic progression by pairing ends
steps.narration: An arithmetic progression has evenly spaced terms. Its average is halfway between the first and last terms, so multiply that average by the number of terms.

steps.title: Recognise a geometric progression by its ratio
steps.narration: A geometric progression multiplies by the same ratio each time. Divide a term by the nonzero term just before it to find the ratio, then count the multiplications from the start.

steps.title: Sum a finite geometric progression
steps.narration: To see the formula, multiply the whole sum by the ratio, then subtract to cancel the overlapping terms. For a ratio of one, each term is the same, so multiply the first term by the number of terms.

steps.title: Sum an infinite geometric progression when it converges
steps.narration: For a nonzero first term, an infinite geometric sum converges only when the magnitude of the ratio is less than one. Then the powers of the ratio approach zero and leave this formula.

steps.title: Check how the terms change
steps.display: Find the sum of the first four terms of 3, 6, 12, … .
steps.narration: The differences are three then six, but both consecutive divisions give two. That makes this a geometric progression.

steps.title: Use the finite sum rule
steps.narration: The question asks for four terms, so use four in the finite sum formula. Put three in as the first term and two as the ratio.

steps.title: Simplify and check by listing
steps.narration: The two minus signs cancel. You can check this short sum by adding three, six, twelve and twenty-four.

steps.title: Count the jumps between the terms
steps.display: The fourth term of an arithmetic progression is 13 and the tenth is 31. Find the twenty-fourth term.
steps.narration: From position four to position ten there are six jumps, all of the same size. The values increase by eighteen across those jumps.

steps.title: Work out the common difference
steps.narration: Divide the total increase by the number of jumps. The progression goes up by three at each step.

steps.title: Jump from the known fourth term
steps.narration: Start at the known fourth term and make twenty more jumps. Add sixty to thirteen to get the twenty-fourth term.

steps.title: Count multiplications from the first term
steps.narration: The first term is already there before any multiplying. The eleventh term therefore takes ten multiplications by two.

steps.title: Divide by one minus the ratio
steps.narration: One minus the ratio is the denominator of the infinite sum. Here divide the first term by one tenth to get ten.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.display: Check the change from term to term
steps.narration: A fixed difference points to an arithmetic progression, and a fixed multiplier points to a geometric progression.

quickCheck.stem: Find the sum to infinity of 1 + \frac{9}{10} + (\frac{9}{10})^{2} + (\frac{9}{10})^{3} + … .

options.why: One tenth is the denominator in the sum formula, so the sum is 1 divided by one tenth.
Nine tenths is the common ratio. The sum already exceeds 1 after adding its first two terms.
This divides the first term by the ratio instead of by 1 minus the ratio.
The ratio is nine tenths, so the infinite sum is 1 ÷ (1 − 0.9) = 10.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: Imagine a tray with a hundred pieces of chin-chin. Take twenty-five. That is twenty-five per cent, a quarter of the tray, or zero point two five of it.

steps.title: Add or subtract equal-sized parts
steps.narration: Turn mixed numbers into improper fractions when it helps. For addition or subtraction, use a common denominator so that all the pieces are the same size.

steps.title: Multiply fractions and divide by the reciprocal
steps.narration: Multiply tops together and bottoms together. To divide by a nonzero fraction, turn that divisor upside down and multiply. With mixed operations, do multiplication and division before addition or subtraction, after any brackets and powers.

steps.title: Use place value for decimals
steps.narration: Align decimal points for addition and subtraction. When multiplying, count the total decimal places of the factors. When dividing, shift both decimal points equally until the divisor is a whole number. Divide the numerator by the denominator to convert a fraction.

steps.title: Round at the requested place
steps.narration: For significant figures, count from the first nonzero digit. For decimal places, count from the decimal point. If the next digit is five or more, round up. Otherwise keep the last digit.

sources.book: Cambridge Excellence in Mathematics Senior Secondary 2 Student’s Book

steps.title: Use the original amount as the percent base
steps.narration: Per cent means out of a hundred. Multiply by the decimal multiplier to find the new amount, and divide by it to recover the original. For profit or loss use the cost, and for percentage error use the true value.

steps.title: Use the original principal for simple interest
steps.narration: Multiply the starting principal by the rate as a decimal and by the time in matching units. For an annual rate use years, then add the interest to the principal if asked for the total.

steps.title: Find the multiplier for an increase
steps.display: A bag costs ₦2,400 after a 20% increase. Find the original price.
steps.narration: The new price includes all of the old price plus one fifth of it. That makes the new price one point two times the old price.

steps.title: Undo the multiplication
steps.narration: Divide the new price by the multiplier. This takes you back to the amount the increase was based on.

steps.title: Check using the original price
steps.narration: Twenty per cent of two thousand is four hundred. Add it to the original price to check that you get the stated new price.

steps.title: Convert the mixed numbers
steps.narration: Convert the mixed numbers so each term is written as one fraction. Multiply each whole number by its denominator before adding its numerator.

steps.title: Do the multiplication first
steps.narration: The middle two fractions are joined by multiplication. Work out that product before subtracting it from the first fraction.

steps.title: Use a common denominator
steps.narration: Thirty is divisible by three, six and five. Rewrite each fraction in thirtieths so the pieces have equal size.

steps.title: Reduce the result
steps.narration: Divide the top and bottom by three. Thirty-nine tenths is three whole ones and nine tenths.

steps.title: Multiply before subtracting
steps.narration: Subtraction has to wait until the product is ready. Group the multiplication first, then use a common denominator for the remaining work.

steps.title: Recover the original percentage base
steps.display: ₦345 is the salary after a 15% rise
steps.narration: The raise was fifteen per cent of the old salary. Dividing by one point one five reverses the increase and brings you back to the old salary.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.display: Track what counts as one whole
steps.narration: Make the parts comparable, and always ask which amount the fraction or percentage is based on.

quickCheck.stem: Calculate the simple interest on ₦1,500 for 8 years at 5% per year.

options.why: ₦5,000 would exceed the original principal several times. The stated rate gives 0.05 × ₦1,500 = ₦75 a year, or ₦600 in eight years.
The annual interest is ₦75, so eight years gives 8 × ₦75 = ₦600.
₦500 falls short of the total because eight yearly payments of ₦75 add up to ₦600.
₦150 is only two years of interest at ₦75 per year.
